# Raman analysis of 2D and layered materials

You read the spectrum; the tools measure. Every number you report comes from a tool output (measured), a
relation applied inside its validity range (inferred, with the relation's source), or a reference entry
(literature, with its source and locator). If none applies, say so under limits.

## Start here: run these commands first (from the folder that holds the data)

Use the validated scripts below; do not write your own baseline, peak-finding or fitting code unless a script
fails or you need a check it does not provide. The scripts and notes are in `C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis`.

```
python "C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/scripts/rl_qc.py" <file>                  # artifacts, Si calibration, resolution
python "C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/scripts/rl_fit.py" <file> --substrate "<substrate>"   # peaks with errors + fit.png
python "C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/scripts/rl_series.py" <f1> <f2> ... --labels <l1> <l2> ... --substrate "<substrate>" --si-correct   # several spectra
python "C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/scripts/rl.py" match_library --positions_cm1 <p1> <p2> ... --intensities <h1> <h2> ... --x_range_cm1 <lo> <hi>
python "C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/scripts/rl.py" lookup_reference_modes --material <name>
python "C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/scripts/rl.py" classify_polarization --path <angle-series file>
python "C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/scripts/rl.py" list_relations --material <name>
python "C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/scripts/rl.py" apply_relation --name <relation> --inputs '{"<input>": <value>}'
```
Then read `C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/reference/materials/<material>.md` (when the material is known or once you have a
candidate) and `C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/reference/artifacts.md`. Always return ranked candidates for an identify task,
even when uncertain: put the uncertainty in the confidence values and the limits, never return an empty list.

## What each script does

- `scripts/rl_qc.py <file>`: quality and condition flags (spikes, saturation, background, Si calibration offset,
  low-wavenumber cutoff, sampling, signal to noise).
- `scripts/rl_fit.py <file> [--substrate SiO2/Si] [--window LO HI] [--min-snr N]`: fitted peak table with
  uncertainties, `peaks.json`, and `fit.png` (data, baseline, components, residual). Look at the plot.
- `scripts/rl_series.py <file1> <file2> ... --labels ... [--substrate SiO2/Si] [--si-correct]`: fits every
  spectrum the same way, tracks each band across spectra (position, width, relative height, shift vs the first
  spectrum with error), separations of the two strongest bands, Si offsets, and `series.png`. Use it whenever
  there is more than one spectrum. Its errors are fit statistics only; add the calibration uncertainty (Si offset
  scatter, typically a few tenths of a cm-1) before calling a shift significant.
- `scripts/rl.py <tool> --help`: `fit_peaks`, `match_library`, `classify_polarization`,
  `lookup_reference_modes`, `list_relations`, `apply_relation`, `load_spectrum`. Outputs carry provenance.

## Workflow

0. **Read the material's literature note first** when the material is known: `C:/Users/sadit/Desktop/P_Projects/Hackathons/OSI Hackathon/skill/ramanlens/skills/raman-analysis/reference/materials/<name>.md`
   (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2, graphene, hBN, black-phosphorus, CrSBr, CrI3-CrBr3, MPS3) plus
   `reference/materials/general-measurement.md` and, for magnets, `magnetic-raman-general.md`. They hold how the
   spectrum changes with thickness, strain, doping, defects, temperature, laser and substrate, the quality
   indicators, the known pitfalls and the questions to ask, each with its source. Interpretation without them is
   guesswork from memory.
1. **Conditions first.** Note laser wavelength, temperature, substrate, polarization geometry, resolution. Many
   conclusions depend on them (`reference/measurement-questions.md`). With a user present, ask for what is missing
   and say why it matters; otherwise state the assumption under limits.
2. **Quality check.** `rl_qc.py`. Spikes are artifacts, never peaks (`reference/artifacts.md`).
3. **Fit.** `rl_fit.py`, then look at `fit.png`. Check weak shoulders and close doublets (2LA(M) next to E2g in
   WS2); refit a window with `--window` when the residual shows structure. Report fitted positions and widths.
4. **Identify.** `rl.py match_library --positions_cm1 ... --intensities ... --x_range_cm1 LO HI` ranks
   candidates from the Computational Raman Database (DFT, frequencies typically 0 to 3 % low, fitted scale per
   candidate) and curated literature tables. Do not stop at the top score: check that the strong predicted modes
   are present and the missing ones are explainable (outside the window, selection rules, resonance). The
   matcher's irreps and space group are the best source for mode labels of uncommon materials. For a stated
   material ("verify"), compare against its reference modes; a wrong hint is common, so say inconsistent when
   strong modes are missing or extra strong bands are unexplained.
5. **Assign.** Each sample peak gets a mode label and irrep with its source: `rl.py lookup_reference_modes
   --material X` for the curated materials (graphene, 2H-MoS2, 2H-WS2, 2H-MoSe2, 2H-WSe2, CrSBr, hBN, black
   phosphorus), the matcher's CRD entry otherwise. Use the irreps of the structure you identified (bulk D6h
   labels for bulk 2H crystals, C3v A1/E for 3R, D3h for a monolayer). Assign Si lines as 'Si substrate'.
6. **Polarization** (angle series only). `rl.py classify_polarization --path <file>` classifies each band
   (isotropic_par_only, isotropic_both, twofold, fourfold, silent). Report the tool's class; use it to check
   irreps (A modes isotropic_par_only and E modes isotropic_both in uniaxial crystals; twofold in in-plane
   anisotropic crystals).
7. **Properties.** Read `reference/relations.md` and `reference/materials.md`, then `rl.py apply_relation`. Report
   layer number, strain, doping or defect density only from a relation (with its source and validity) or a
   stated rule from the notes. Name properties `layers`, `defect_level`, `L_D_nm`, `strain_sign`,
   `doping_type`, `phase` where they apply.
8. **Literature** (when the Valency and iopic-bond tools are available). Form the hypothesis first; never search by
   peak positions. See `reference/literature.md`: find the paper, view its reference spectrum figure, compare.
9. **Interpret changes** (several spectra, or a known material). Run `rl_series.py`; then for each change ask
   which mechanisms in the material note produce it (thickness, strain, doping, defects, heating, calibration,
   resonance) and which observable separates them (e.g. a rigid shift of all lines including Si is calibration;
   A1g-only shift in MoS2 points to doping, E2g shift with splitting to strain; graphene G broadening separates
   stage 1 from stage 2 defects). State the most likely reading, the alternatives, and the measurement that would
   decide between them.
10. **Report.** Ranked candidates with evidence, peaks with provenance and source, properties with relation and
   source, artifacts, citations (only sources you used), and limits: what the data cannot tell, rejected
   hypotheses, relations that did not apply and why.

## Expert habits

- One spectrum rarely fixes layer number alone; name the observable and its threshold.
- Laser heating, strain and doping shift lines by similar amounts; check calibration before reading 1 to 2 cm-1.
- Intensity ratios depend on substrate interference and laser energy; absolute intensity is not layer number.
- Resonant excitation changes relative intensities and activates second-order bands; check the laser against the
  material's excitons before calling a band unexpected.
- When something looks odd, say what it looks like and what would distinguish the explanations.

# MoS2: expert Raman notes

Scope: 2H-MoS2 (and the 3R polytype where noted). Numbers appear only where they were read in the cited source;
the locator says where. "Consensus" means several independent sources agree; "single source" means one paper.
Positions move 1 to 3 cm-1 with calibration, substrate, strain and doping: reason from differences and trends.

## Signature and irreps
- Bulk 2H (D6h): Raman-active A1g, E1g, E2g (two); E1g is forbidden in backscattering from the basal plane
  (Zhang X. et al. 2015, Chem. Soc. Rev. 44, 2757, arXiv:1502.00701, p.3 and p.6).
- Monolayer (D3h): E2g1 becomes E', A1g becomes A1'; odd N is D3h, even N is D3d, so labels change with parity
  (Zhang X. 2015, p.3, p.7).
- Main lines at 514.5 nm on 285 nm SiO2/Si: 1L E' 384.0, A1' 403.1 cm-1 (separation 19.1); bulk 382.2 / 407.4
  (25.2) (Lee C. et al. 2010, ACS Nano 4, 2695, arXiv:1005.2509, Fig. 2b). Consensus.
- Widths: E2g1 about 2.1 cm-1; A1g 3 to 6 cm-1, broadening from 6L to 2L (Lee 2010, p.4).
- Bulk interlayer shear mode E2g2 near 32 cm-1 (Zhang X. 2015, p.11).

## Thickness
- E2g1 softens and A1g stiffens with N; the separation is the standard layer counter up to about 4L
  (Lee 2010, Fig. 2b). It holds on SiO2, hBN, mica, Gel-Film, Au and few-layer graphene (Buscema M. et al. 2014,
  arXiv:1311.3869, p.4). Consensus.
- Above about 5L the separation saturates; use the low-frequency shear (C) and layer-breathing (LB) modes, whose
  positions follow a linear-chain model with different branches for odd and even N
  (Zhang X. et al. 2013, PRB 87, 115413, arXiv:1212.6796, abstract and Fig. 2; review Fig. 5, p.8).
- Stacking: 2H vs 3R bilayers differ in the low-frequency modes, not in the E/A pair
  (Ranjuna M. K. et al. 2023, Sci. Rep. 13, 16418, doi:10.1038/s41598-023-43756-w, p.2, Fig. 1d to f).
- Intensity is not a thickness measure on its own: MoS2 and Si intensities oscillate with N through optical
  interference; the Si-normalized MoS2 signal is monotonic and can be used (Li S.-L. et al., arXiv:1308.3835,
  abstract; companion of ACS Nano 6, 7381, 2012).

## Strain and doping
- Uniaxial tensile strain: E' softens about -4.5 cm-1/% (1L) and splits into E'+ and E'-; A1' shows no
  measurable shift (Conley H. J. et al. 2013, Nano Lett. 13, 3626, arXiv:1305.3880, text). Consensus.
- Electron doping (electrolyte gate): 1L A1g softens about 4 cm-1 and broadens about 6 cm-1 at 1.8e13 cm-2;
  E2g1 moves about 0.6 cm-1 (Chakraborty B. et al. 2012, PRB 85, 161403, arXiv:1206.1758, text).
- Rule of thumb: A1' shift with broadening points to doping; E' shift, especially with splitting, to strain.
- Substrate doping: A1g of 1L stiffens by up to about 2 cm-1 from SiO2 (lowest) to hBN (highest) while E2g1
  barely moves, attributed to lower electron density on hBN (Buscema 2014, p.7, Fig. 4c).
- Transfer can shift peaks through strain release and interface effects (Zhang X. et al. 2025, Nat. Commun. 16,
  4468, doi:10.1038/s41467-025-59803-1, p.4); monolayer separation is "typically about 20 cm-1" there.

## Defects and quality
- LA(M) near 227 cm-1 is the main defect-activated band; I(LA)/I(first order) scales with defect density
  (Mignuzzi S. et al. 2015, PRB 91, 195411, abstract). Quantitative L_D calibration not verified here.
- Few-layer modes near 286 and 471 cm-1 (forbidden for 1L backscattering) are intrinsic resonant modes, not
  defects; strongest at UV excitation such as 3.8 eV (Scheuschner N. et al. 2015, PRB 91, 235409,
  arXiv:1503.08980, pp.8 to 9).
- Sulfur vacancies show up more in widths and relative intensities than in positions at high temperature
  (Ranjuna 2023, p.9). Narrow lines (E2g1 about 2 cm-1, Lee 2010) indicate good crystals.

## Temperature and heating
- Both main modes redshift on heating. First-order coefficients: few-layer -1.32e-2 (E2g1) and -1.23e-2 (A1g)
  cm-1/K (Sahoo S. et al. 2013, J. Phys. Chem. C, doi:10.1021/jp402509w, arXiv:1302.5865, p.6); 1L
  -0.013 (E2g) and -0.016 (A1g) cm-1/K (Lanzillo N. et al. 2013, APL, doi:10.1063/1.4819337, Table I);
  1L on SiO2 is nonlinear below room temperature, literature values -0.011 to -0.017 cm-1/K
  (Taube A. et al. 2014, ACS AMI, doi:10.1021/am502359k, Table 1, p.5). Consensus on sign and order; values
  scatter with substrate and sample.
- Laser heating redshifts and broadens both modes (Ranjuna 2023, pp.5 to 6, Fig. 6). On a suspended few-layer
  flake A1g shifts about 5.4 cm-1/mW (Sahoo 2013, p.10): suspended flakes heat strongly.
- Damage: 10 mW at 514 nm, scanned, sublimates upper layers of multilayer MoS2 on SiO2 and leaves a monolayer,
  because the bottom layer is heat-sunk to the substrate (Castellanos-Gomez A. et al. 2012, Nano Lett. 12, 3187,
  arXiv:1206.4323, p.3).
- Modest laser exposure in air can also increase Raman intensity 3 to 5 times, harden A1g by 1.4 cm-1 and soften
  E2g1 by 1 cm-1 (attributed to defect healing) (Bera A. et al. 2017, arXiv:1707.09386, abstract). So repeated
  scans of one spot are not independent.

## Excitation wavelength and resonance
- 633 nm (near the A exciton) gives resonant spectra rich in second-order bands that evolve with N: 2LA(M)
  near 450, A1g(M)-LA(M) near 179, a B1u Davydov partner of A1g near 403 that grows with N, and a 420 cm-1
  band (B2g2+E1u-type combination) that is absent in 1L (Zhang X. 2015, Fig. 12, pp.13 to 14; 1L assignments
  in Table III, p.15). Off resonance (514, 532 nm) the
  spectrum is mainly E' and A1'.
- UV (325 nm) enhances combination modes 750 to 840 cm-1 (Zhang X. 2015, p.15).
- Consequence: peak lists and intensity ratios are only comparable at the same laser line.

## Polarization and substrate
- Backscattering, linear: A1g/A1' appears in XX and vanishes in YX; E2g1/E' is present in both with equal
  intensity (Zhang X. 2015, p.6 to 7, Fig. 3c). Use this to separate overlapping modes.
- Substrate also modulates intensity through interference (Buscema 2014, abstract; Li arXiv:1308.3835).
- Mica has a Bg mode that can overlap A1g (Buscema 2014, p.7).

## Pitfalls and artifacts
- Spectral resolution: Lee 2010 used 2.7 cm-1; the 1L-2L separation step is about 2 cm-1, comparable.
- 3R and 1T polytypes break the 2H rules (see materials.md); check stacking before applying the separation.
- Calibrate with Si (about 520 cm-1) in the same spectrum; report the laser line.
- Doping and strain both move A1': a single spectrum cannot separate all causes; say so.

## What to ask
- Laser wavelength, power at the sample, spot size, objective; was power varied?
- Substrate (SiO2 thickness), suspended or supported, encapsulated (hBN), transferred or as-grown.
- Exfoliated or CVD; age and storage; any gating or illumination history.
- Polarization configuration; temperature and environment (air, vacuum).
- Grating, resolution and calibration reference.

## Reference figures
- Lee 2010, arXiv:1005.2509, Fig. 2a,b: spectra and E2g1/A1g positions vs layer number (514.5 nm).
- Zhang X. 2013, arXiv:1212.6796, Fig. 2: 5L, 6L, bulk spectra incl. low-frequency modes, XX vs YX.
- Zhang X. 2015, arXiv:1502.00701, Fig. 12: resonant (633 nm) spectra of 1, 2, 4, 7L and bulk.
- Conley 2013, arXiv:1305.3880, Fig. 2: E' splitting under uniaxial strain.
------
# Artifacts and red flags in Raman spectra of 2D materials

Each entry: what it looks like, how to tell it from a real band, what to do. Sources in brackets.

## Cosmic-ray spikes
- One to three pixels wide, far narrower than any phonon line at the instrument resolution, present in one
  acquisition only. Real lines have the instrument's minimum width and repeat across accumulations or angles.
- Remove before fitting (modified z-score on the first difference: Whitaker and Hayes, Chemom. Intell. Lab. Syst.
  179, 82, 2018). In an angle series, replace spike pixels from the most similar frame (Barton and Hennelly, Appl.
  Spectrosc. 73, 893, 2019). List them under artifacts, never under peaks.

## Silicon substrate
- First-order Si line near 520.7 cm-1 (a widely used calibration convention; check the offset of the fitted
  position and flag a calibration problem when it exceeds about 1 cm-1; 520 to 520.9 is reported in practice, Lee
  et al. 2010 and Castellanos-Gomez et al. 2014). Second-order Si features near 950 and 980 cm-1 (Gillet et al.
  2017, arXiv 1708.05874, Fig. 1) and a 2TA band computed near 300 cm-1 (same paper, DFPT) can be mistaken for
  sample modes. Brillouin scattering from Si gives a line near
  4.5 cm-1 in ultra-low-frequency setups (Zhang et al., PRB 87, 115413, 2013).
- Assign these as 'Si substrate'. A strong Si line with weak sample bands suggests a thin flake.

## Calibration
- First-order wavelength calibration errors of 5 to 7 cm-1 have been reported (Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1024,
  2012). Shifts of 1 to 3 cm-1 (layer number, strain, doping) are only meaningful after a calibration check.

## Background
- Broad fluorescence or photoluminescence slopes; remove with an asymmetric least-squares baseline (arPLS or
  asPLS). For broad bands (disordered carbon D and G, amorphous phases) a global baseline can eat real signal: fit
  a local linear background together with the peaks. A Breit-Wigner-Fano line shape can absorb a background slope;
  compare line shapes by BIC.

## Low-wavenumber cutoff
- Notch and edge filters block the region near the laser line (Bragg notch filters reach about 5 to 10 cm-1,
  Zhang et al. 2013). A missing shear or breathing mode below the cutoff is not evidence of absence.

## Plasma lines
- Laser plasma lines have a fixed absolute wavelength, so their Raman shift changes when the laser changes; they
  are very narrow and do not belong to the sample. Suspect them when a narrow line has no assignment.

## Laser heating
- Phonon lines soften and broaden with temperature. Graphene G shifts about -0.016 cm-1/K (Calizo et al., Nano
  Lett. 7, 2645, 2007); 1L WS2 about -0.0093 (E) and -0.0122 (A1g) cm-1/K (Huang et al., Sci. Rep. 2016);
  few-layer MoS2 about -0.013 and -0.012 cm-1/K (Sahoo et al., arXiv 1302.5865). A power series is the test.

## Substrate interference
- On SiO2/Si, absolute intensities and intensity ratios depend on oxide thickness and laser wavelength: graphene
  I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al., PRB 80, 125422, 2009).
  Never read layer number from absolute intensity or from I(2D)/I(G) without the substrate stack.

## Resonance
- Near an excitonic resonance, second-order bands can exceed first-order ones. WS2 at 514 to 532 nm: 2LA(M) lies
  about 4 cm-1 below E2g and overlaps it (Berkdemir et al., Sci. Rep. 3, 1755, 2013; Mitioglu et al., PRB 89,
  245442, 2014). Fit both or the E2g position and layer count are wrong.

## Saturation and clipping
- A flat-topped peak or values at the detector maximum: the peak shape and intensity are wrong; ask for a shorter
  exposure.

  1L on SiO2 is nonlinear below room temperature, literature values -0.011 to -0.017 cm-1/K
  (Taube A. et al. 2014, ACS AMI, doi:10.1021/am502359k, Table 1, p.5). Consensus on sign and order; values
  scatter with substrate and sample.
- Laser heating redshifts and broadens both modes (Ranjuna 2023, pp.5 to 6, Fig. 6). On a suspended few-layer
  flake A1g shifts about 5.4 cm-1/mW (Sahoo 2013, p.10): suspended flakes heat strongly.
- Damage: 10 mW at 514 nm, scanned, sublimates upper layers of multilayer MoS2 on SiO2 and leaves a monolayer,
  because the bottom layer is heat-sunk to the substrate (Castellanos-Gomez A. et al. 2012, Nano Lett. 12, 3187,
  arXiv:1206.4323, p.3).
- Modest laser exposure in air can also increase Raman intensity 3 to 5 times, harden A1g by 1.4 cm-1 and soften
  E2g1 by 1 cm-1 (attributed to defect healing) (Bera A. et al. 2017, arXiv:1707.09386, abstract). So repeated
  scans of one spot are not independent.

## Excitation wavelength and resonance
- 633 nm (near the A exciton) gives resonant spectra rich in second-order bands that evolve with N: 2LA(M)
  near 450, A1g(M)-LA(M) near 179, a B1u Davydov partner of A1g near 403 that grows with N, and a 420 cm-1
  band (B2g2+E1u-type combination) that is absent in 1L (Zhang X. 2015, Fig. 12, pp.13 to 14; 1L assignments
  in Table III, p.15). Off resonance (514, 532 nm) the
  spectrum is mainly E' and A1'.
- UV (325 nm) enhances combination modes 750 to 840 cm-1 (Zhang X. 2015, p.15).
- Consequence: peak lists and intensity ratios are only comparable at the same laser line.

## Polarization and substrate
- Backscattering, linear: A1g/A1' appears in XX and vanishes in YX; E2g1/E' is present in both with equal
  intensity (Zhang X. 2015, p.6 to 7, Fig. 3c). Use this to separate overlapping modes.
- Substrate also modulates intensity through interference (Buscema 2014, abstract; Li arXiv:1308.3835).
- Mica has a Bg mode that can overlap A1g (Buscema 2014, p.7).

## Pitfalls and artifacts
- Spectral resolution: Lee 2010 used 2.7 cm-1; the 1L-2L separation step is about 2 cm-1, comparable.
- 3R and 1T polytypes break the 2H rules (see materials.md); check stacking before applying the separation.
- Calibrate with Si (about 520 cm-1) in the same spectrum; report the laser line.
- Doping and strain both move A1': a single spectrum cannot separate all causes; say so.

## What to ask
- Laser wavelength, power at the sample, spot size, objective; was power varied?
- Substrate (SiO2 thickness), suspended or supported, encapsulated (hBN), transferred or as-grown.
- Exfoliated or CVD; age and storage; any gating or illumination history.
- Polarization configuration; temperature and environment (air, vacuum).
- Grating, resolution and calibration reference.

## Reference figures
- Lee 2010, arXiv:1005.2509, Fig. 2a,b: spectra and E2g1/A1g positions vs layer number (514.5 nm).
- Zhang X. 2013, arXiv:1212.6796, Fig. 2: 5L, 6L, bulk spectra incl. low-frequency modes, XX vs YX.
- Zhang X. 2015, arXiv:1502.00701, Fig. 12: resonant (633 nm) spectra of 1, 2, 4, 7L and bulk.
- Conley 2013, arXiv:1305.3880, Fig. 2: E' splitting under uniaxial strain.
------
# Artifacts and red flags in Raman spectra of 2D materials

Each entry: what it looks like, how to tell it from a real band, what to do. Sources in brackets.

## Cosmic-ray spikes
- One to three pixels wide, far narrower than any phonon line at the instrument resolution, present in one
  acquisition only. Real lines have the instrument's minimum width and repeat across accumulations or angles.
- Remove before fitting (modified z-score on the first difference: Whitaker and Hayes, Chemom. Intell. Lab. Syst.
  179, 82, 2018). In an angle series, replace spike pixels from the most similar frame (Barton and Hennelly, Appl.
  Spectrosc. 73, 893, 2019). List them under artifacts, never under peaks.

## Silicon substrate
- First-order Si line near 520.7 cm-1 (a widely used calibration convention; check the offset of the fitted
  position and flag a calibration problem when it exceeds about 1 cm-1; 520 to 520.9 is reported in practice, Lee
  et al. 2010 and Castellanos-Gomez et al. 2014). Second-order Si features near 950 and 980 cm-1 (Gillet et al.
  2017, arXiv 1708.05874, Fig. 1) and a 2TA band computed near 300 cm-1 (same paper, DFPT) can be mistaken for
  sample modes. Brillouin scattering from Si gives a line near
  4.5 cm-1 in ultra-low-frequency setups (Zhang et al., PRB 87, 115413, 2013).
- Assign these as 'Si substrate'. A strong Si line with weak sample bands suggests a thin flake.

## Calibration
- First-order wavelength calibration errors of 5 to 7 cm-1 have been reported (Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1024,
  2012). Shifts of 1 to 3 cm-1 (layer number, strain, doping) are only meaningful after a calibration check.

## Background
- Broad fluorescence or photoluminescence slopes; remove with an asymmetric least-squares baseline (arPLS or
  asPLS). For broad bands (disordered carbon D and G, amorphous phases) a global baseline can eat real signal: fit
  a local linear background together with the peaks. A Breit-Wigner-Fano line shape can absorb a background slope;
  compare line shapes by BIC.

## Low-wavenumber cutoff
- Notch and edge filters block the region near the laser line (Bragg notch filters reach about 5 to 10 cm-1,
  Zhang et al. 2013). A missing shear or breathing mode below the cutoff is not evidence of absence.

## Plasma lines
- Laser plasma lines have a fixed absolute wavelength, so their Raman shift changes when the laser changes; they
  are very narrow and do not belong to the sample. Suspect them when a narrow line has no assignment.

## Laser heating
- Phonon lines soften and broaden with temperature. Graphene G shifts about -0.016 cm-1/K (Calizo et al., Nano
  Lett. 7, 2645, 2007); 1L WS2 about -0.0093 (E) and -0.0122 (A1g) cm-1/K (Huang et al., Sci. Rep. 2016);
  few-layer MoS2 about -0.013 and -0.012 cm-1/K (Sahoo et al., arXiv 1302.5865). A power series is the test.

## Substrate interference
- On SiO2/Si, absolute intensities and intensity ratios depend on oxide thickness and laser wavelength: graphene
  I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al., PRB 80, 125422, 2009).
  Never read layer number from absolute intensity or from I(2D)/I(G) without the substrate stack.

## Resonance
- Near an excitonic resonance, second-order bands can exceed first-order ones. WS2 at 514 to 532 nm: 2LA(M) lies
  about 4 cm-1 below E2g and overlaps it (Berkdemir et al., Sci. Rep. 3, 1755, 2013; Mitioglu et al., PRB 89,
  245442, 2014). Fit both or the E2g position and layer count are wrong.

## Saturation and clipping
- A flat-topped peak or values at the detector maximum: the peak shape and intensity are wrong; ask for a shorter
  exposure.

A calibration offset of -0.7 cm-1 is the same in every spectrum, so it does not affect the separations. Si-normalised intensity supports the order B < A < D ≲ C, and the A1g width trend is consistent with D being thinner than C. The exact layer count for D and C needs AFM or the low-frequency shear/breathing modes (<150 cm-1, outside this window).

observations.finding: Flake B is a monolayer.
observations.evidence: Raw Lorentzian fit: E2g1 383.90 ± 0.03, A1g 403.14 ± 0.10 (local refit 403.13 ± 0.10), separation 19.23 ± 0.11 cm-1. A1g FWHM about 4.8 to 5.0 cm-1, E2g1 FWHM 2.04. These match the 1L entry (384.0/403.1, Δ19.1). Si line is the strongest feature (E/Si height 0.40).

observations.finding: Flake A is a bilayer.
observations.evidence: E2g1 383.37 ± 0.02, A1g 404.80 ± 0.07, separation 21.43 to 21.45 ± 0.08 cm-1 (table 2L 21.4). A1g is the broadest band of the set (FWHM 6.2 to 6.4 cm-1), as expected for 2L (A1g broadens from 6L to 2L). E/Si height ratio about 0.97.

observations.finding: Flake D is about 4L (moderate confidence), possibly 4 to 6L. It is not clearly bulk.
observations.evidence: E2g1 382.37 ± 0.01, A1g 406.64 ± 0.03, separation 24.26 ± 0.03 cm-1 (table: 4L 24.3, bulk 25.2). A1g FWHM 4.5 to 4.6 cm-1 versus 2.9 in C. E/Si height about 2.7. The separation saturates above about 4 to 5L, so the 0.9 cm-1 gap to bulk is the only discriminator.
observations.source: Lee 2010, Fig. 2b; Zhang X. et al. 2015, Chem. Soc. Rev. 44, 2757 (saturation above about 5L, use low-frequency modes)

observations.finding: Flake C is bulk-like (thick, at least about 5L and plausibly tens of nm).
observations.evidence: E2g1 382.24 ± 0.04, A1g 407.30 ± 0.06, separation 25.06 to 25.07 ± 0.07 cm-1 (bulk 25.2). A1g FWHM 2.9 cm-1, the narrowest of the set and close to the E2g1 width 2.1 to 2.2. Compared with D, the Si line is relatively weaker.
observations.source: Lee 2010, Fig. 2b; Li S.-L. et al., arXiv:1308.3835 (Si-normalised MoS2 signal grows monotonically with thickness)

observations.finding: Thickness ordering is consistent across independent observables.
observations.evidence: A1g position (raw): 403.1 (B) < 404.8 (A) < 406.6 (D) < 407.3 (C). E2g1 (raw): 383.9 > 383.4 > 382.4 ≈ 382.2. caveats: The separation table is calibrated for 2H, exfoliated flakes on 285 nm SiO2/Si at 514.5 nm, and for 2.7 cm-1 resolution. Those match your conditions, but 3L, 4L and bulk differ by only about 1 cm-1, so D is not firmly 4L (4 to 6L is possible) and C 'bulk' only means at least about 5L.

Strain or doping can shift A1g/E2g1 by 1 to 2 cm-1 and so mimic one layer difference; the absolute shifts in D vs C (A1g 0.7 cm-1 lower in D) could in principle be doping or substrate effects rather than thickness. The A1g width difference (4.6 vs 2.9) supports a thickness reading, but one spectrum per flake cannot prove it.

Laser heating redshifts both modes by about 0.012 to 0.013 cm-1/K and broadens them. A hot spot would soften both and increase widths; the narrow, thickness-ordered lines argue against strong heating, but no power series was measured. A repeated exposure can also change intensity and A1g by about 1 cm-1 (Bera 2017). Suspended or thin flakes heat more.

Absolute intensity is not layer number. Interference on 285 nm SiO2 modulates it, and exposure, focus and power can differ between spectra (C is weak overall). Only the Si-normalised ratio is a usable (monotonic) trend, and it cannot separate D from C.

The weak Si line in C: this could mean very thick MoS2 absorbing both beams, but also a defocused/off-flake-edge spot or another substrate. With SNR about 19 the Si position and width are unreliable and C's own calibration is untested.
The fit table lists broad components at 222 cm-1 (B) and 321/330 cm-1 (D); these are baseline/background artifacts, not modes (errors as large as the values).
The low-wavenumber cutoff (data start at 150 cm-1) removes the shear (about 32 cm-1) and layer-breathing modes, which are the tool for 3 to 6L and bulk and for 2H vs 3R stacking.
Natural molybdenite flakes may carry impurities, and a thin hole/lens or contamination could affect widths; none was visible, but heterogeneity within a flake was not mapped.
questions_for_user: What are the laser power at the sample and the acquisition time for each flake? Power differences change heating (redshift) and the absolute intensity, which could explain the weak C spectrum and a possible 1 to 2 cm-1 shift.
Was the spectrometer calibrated (Si at 520.7?) before each measurement? The Si line is at 519.99 to 520.02 in three spectra (-0.7 cm-1) and unusable in C, so I cannot confirm C's calibration.
Was the Si peak recorded at the same spot on C? Why is it nearly absent (a very thick flake, a different substrate region, an off-focus spot)?

Can you measure ultralow-frequency Raman (below 150 cm-1: shear about 32 cm-1 and breathing modes) or take AFM/optical contrast on C and D? These decide 4L vs 5 to 6L vs bulk, which the E2g1/A1g pair cannot.
Was the same spot measured repeatedly, and was a power series taken? Repeated exposure in air changes intensity and A1g (Bera 2017), and a power series tests heating.
Are there PL spectra, or other spectra at 633 nm or in the 1.8 to 1.9 eV range, available? They would give a thickness-independent check (A-exciton PL quenches with thickness).

Low-frequency modes (below 150 cm-1) are not covered, so layer number above about 4L, odd/even assignment and 2H vs 3R stacking cannot be tested.

One spectrum per flake: no mapping, no polarization, no power series, so uniformity, heating, strain (E2g1 splitting needs polarization) and doping cannot be separated rigorously, and they are only constrained by the absence of anomalies.

Only 514.5 nm: second-order and resonant bands (LA(M), 2LA near 450, 286/471 cm-1) are weak off resonance, so the absence of the LA(M) band is a weaker proof of low defect density than a 633 nm or UV measurement would be. A calibration offset of -0.7 cm-1 is the same in every spectrum, so it does not affect the separations. Si-normalised intensity supports the order B < A < D ≲ C, and the A1g width trend is consistent with D being thinner than C. The exact layer count for D and C needs AFM or the low-frequency shear/breathing modes (<150 cm-1, outside this window).

observations.finding: Flake B is a monolayer.
observations.evidence: Raw Lorentzian fit: E2g1 383.90 ± 0.03, A1g 403.14 ± 0.10 (local refit 403.13 ± 0.10), separation 19.23 ± 0.11 cm-1. A1g FWHM about 4.8 to 5.0 cm-1, E2g1 FWHM 2.04. These match the 1L entry (384.0/403.1, Δ19.1). Si line is the strongest feature (E/Si height 0.40).
observations.source: Lee et al. 2010, ACS Nano 4, 2695, Fig. 2b (via the mos2_layer_number_from_separation relation, confidence high)

observations.finding: Flake A is a bilayer.
observations.evidence: E2g1 383.37 ± 0.02, A1g 404.80 ± 0.07, separation 21.43 to 21.45 ± 0.08 cm-1 (table 2L 21.4). A1g is the broadest band of the set (FWHM 6.2 to 6.4 cm-1), as expected for 2L (A1g broadens from 6L to 2L). E/Si height ratio about 0.97.

observations.finding: Flake D is about 4L (moderate confidence), possibly 4 to 6L. It is not clearly bulk.
observations.evidence: E2g1 382.37 ± 0.01, A1g 406.64 ± 0.03, separation 24.26 ± 0.03 cm-1 (table: 4L 24.3, bulk 25.2). A1g FWHM 4.5 to 4.6 cm-1 versus 2.9 in C. E/Si height about 2.7. The separation saturates above about 4 to 5L, so the 0.9 cm-1 gap to bulk is the only discriminator.
observations.source: Lee 2010, Fig. 2b; Zhang X. et al. 2015, Chem. Soc. Rev. 44, 2757 (saturation above about 5L, use low-frequency modes)

observations.finding: Flake C is bulk-like (thick, at least about 5L and plausibly tens of nm).
observations.evidence: E2g1 382.24 ± 0.04, A1g 407.30 ± 0.06, separation 25.06 to 25.07 ± 0.07 cm-1 (bulk 25.2). A1g FWHM 2.9 cm-1, the narrowest of the set and close to the E2g1 width 2.1 to 2.2. The Si line is nearly extinguished: height about 97 against the MoS2 E2g1 at about 340, and the fit gives 519.94 ± 0.29, FWHM 4.5 (poorly constrained). Compared with D, the Si line is relatively weaker.
observations.source: Lee 2010, Fig. 2b; Li S.-L. et al., arXiv:1308.3835 (Si-normalised MoS2 signal grows monotonically with thickness)

observations.finding: Thickness ordering is consistent across independent observables.
observations.evidence: A1g position (raw): 403.1 (B) < 404.8 (A) < 406.6 (D) < 407.3 (C). E2g1 (raw): 383.9 > 383.4 > 382.4 ≈ 382.2. E2g1 FWHM is the same in all four (2.04 to 2.18, near the 2.7 cm-1 resolution limit). Si-normalised E2g1 height: 0.40, 0.97, 2.7, 3.5. The positions agree with Lee 2010 values to better than 1 cm-1.

observations.finding: Crystal quality is good and no defect or strain signature is resolved.
observations.evidence: No LA(M) at about 227 cm-1 above noise in any spectrum (maxima inside the noise of about 20 counts; the local noise is 18 to 24 counts). No E2g1 splitting or broadening: E2g1 FWHM about 2.1 in all four. No 286 or 471 cm-1 band (expected off-resonance at 514.5 nm). 2LA(M) near 450 not seen.
observations.source: Mignuzzi et al. 2015, PRB 91, 195411 (LA(M) as defect band); Scheuschner et al. 2015, PRB 91, 235409 (286/471 are intrinsic resonant modes)

observations.finding: The broad components that the automatic fit reports are artifacts, not phonons.
observations.evidence: B: 222 cm-1, FWHM 65, position error 48. D: 321 and 330 cm-1, FWHM 33 to 38, errors 16 to 25 cm-1 and with fit residual structure. The error bars are as large as the values. Local refits (340 to 440 cm-1, linear background) give the same sharp lines without them. D also has a higher flat background (about 680 against about 400 in the others), which is offset or baseline, not a band.

observations.finding: Cosmic-ray spike in C.
observations.evidence: 1 spike removed at 265.1 cm-1 (one to two pixels). C has low SNR (strongest band about 19 times noise; others 56 to 111).

observations.finding: Calibration: all four spectra sit about 0.7 cm-1 low against Si.
observations.evidence: Si line at 520.02 (A), 520.00 (B), 519.99 (D), i.e. offset -0.68, -0.70, -0.71 from 520.7 cm-1. C has no usable Si line (519.94 ± 0.29, weak). The offset is rigid, so separations are unaffected, but absolute E2g1/A1g positions are 0.7 cm-1 low (Si-corrected values are 0.7 higher: for example B 384.6/403.8).

caveats: The separation table is calibrated for 2H, exfoliated flakes on 285 nm SiO2/Si at 514.5 nm, and for 2.7 cm-1 resolution. Those match your conditions, but 3L, 4L and bulk differ by only about 1 cm-1, so D is not firmly 4L (4 to 6L is possible) and C 'bulk' only means at least about 5L.

Strain or doping can shift A1g/E2g1 by 1 to 2 cm-1 and so mimic one layer difference; the absolute shifts in D vs C (A1g 0.7 cm-1 lower in D) could in principle be doping or substrate effects rather than thickness. The A1g width difference (4.6 vs 2.9) supports a thickness reading, but one spectrum per flake cannot prove it.

Laser heating redshifts both modes by about 0.012 to 0.013 cm-1/K and broadens them. A hot spot would soften both and increase widths; the narrow, thickness-ordered lines argue against strong heating, but no power series was measured. A repeated exposure can also change intensity and A1g by about 1 cm-1 (Bera 2017). Suspended or thin flakes heat more.

Absolute intensity is not layer number. Interference on 285 nm SiO2 modulates it, and exposure, focus and power can differ between spectra (C is weak overall). Only the Si-normalised ratio is a usable (monotonic) trend, and it cannot separate D from C.

The weak Si line in C: this could mean very thick MoS2 absorbing both beams, but also a defocused/off-flake-edge spot or another substrate. With SNR about 19 the Si position and width are unreliable and C's own calibration is untested.
The fit table lists broad components at 222 cm-1 (B) and 321/330 cm-1 (D); these are baseline/background artifacts, not modes (errors as large as the values).
The low-wavenumber cutoff (data start at 150 cm-1) removes the shear (about 32 cm-1) and layer-breathing modes, which are the tool for 3 to 6L and bulk and for 2H vs 3R stacking.
Natural molybdenite flakes may carry impurities, and a thin hole/lens or contamination could affect widths; none was visible, but heterogeneity within a flake was not mapped.
questions_for_user: What are the laser power at the sample and the acquisition time for each flake? Power differences change heating (redshift) and the absolute intensity, which could explain the weak C spectrum and a possible 1 to 2 cm-1 shift.
Was the spectrometer calibrated (Si at 520.7?) before each measurement? The Si line is at 519.99 to 520.02 in three spectra (-0.7 cm-1) and unusable in C, so I cannot confirm C's calibration.
Was the Si peak recorded at the same spot on C? Why is it nearly absent (a very thick flake, a different substrate region, an off-focus spot)?

Can you measure ultralow-frequency Raman (below 150 cm-1: shear about 32 cm-1 and breathing modes) or take AFM/optical contrast on C and D? These decide 4L vs 5 to 6L vs bulk, which the E2g1/A1g pair cannot.
Was the same spot measured repeatedly, and was a power series taken? Repeated exposure in air changes intensity and A1g (Bera 2017), and a power series tests heating.
Are there PL spectra, or other spectra at 633 nm or in the 1.8 to 1.9 eV range, available? They would give a thickness-independent check (A-exciton PL quenches with thickness).

limits: No thickness measurement independent of Raman (AFM, optical contrast, PL) exists here, so the layer numbers rest on one relation tabulated from one paper; D and C are not resolved from each other beyond 'at least 4L'.
Low-frequency modes (below 150 cm-1) are not covered, so layer number above about 4L, odd/even assignment and 2H vs 3R stacking cannot be tested.

One spectrum per flake: no mapping, no polarization, no power series, so uniformity, heating, strain (E2g1 splitting needs polarization) and doping cannot be separated rigorously, and they are only constrained by the absence of anomalies.

Only 514.5 nm: second-order and resonant bands (LA(M), 2LA near 450, 286/471 cm-1) are weak off resonance, so the absence of the LA(M) band is a weaker proof of low defect density than a 633 nm or UV measurement would be. No quantitative defect density (L_D) calibration was applied (not verified for MoS2).
C has no reliable Si reference (519.94 ± 0.29 cm-1), so its absolute positions are less certain than those of A, B and D, although its separation does not depend on calibration.
A1g width and Si-normalised intensity are used as supporting trends only; I did not apply a quantitative relation for them.

caveats: The separation table is calibrated for 2H, exfoliated flakes on 285 nm SiO2/Si at 514.5 nm, and for 2.7 cm-1 resolution. Those match your conditions, but 3L, 4L and bulk differ by only about 1 cm-1, so D is not firmly 4L (4 to 6L is possible) and C 'bulk' only means at least about 5L.

Strain or doping can shift A1g/E2g1 by 1 to 2 cm-1 and so mimic one layer difference; the absolute shifts in D vs C (A1g 0.7 cm-1 lower in D) could in principle be doping or substrate effects rather than thickness. The A1g width difference (4.6 vs 2.9) supports a thickness reading, but one spectrum per flake cannot prove it.

Laser heating redshifts both modes by about 0.012 to 0.013 cm-1/K and broadens them. A hot spot would soften both and increase widths; the narrow, thickness-ordered lines argue against strong heating, but no power series was measured. A repeated exposure can also change intensity and A1g by about 1 cm-1 (Bera 2017). Suspended or thin flakes heat more.

Absolute intensity is not layer number. Interference on 285 nm SiO2 modulates it, and exposure, focus and power can differ between spectra (C is weak overall). Only the Si-normalised ratio is a usable (monotonic) trend, and it cannot separate D from C.

The weak Si line in C: this could mean very thick MoS2 absorbing both beams, but also a defocused/off-flake-edge spot or another substrate. With SNR about 19 the Si position and width are unreliable and C's own calibration is untested.
The fit table lists broad components at 222 cm-1 (B) and 321/330 cm-1 (D); these are baseline/background artifacts, not modes (errors as large as the values).
The low-wavenumber cutoff (data start at 150 cm-1) removes the shear (about 32 cm-1) and layer-breathing modes, which are the tool for 3 to 6L and bulk and for 2H vs 3R stacking.
Natural molybdenite flakes may carry impurities, and a thin hole/lens or contamination could affect widths; none was visible, but heterogeneity within a flake was not mapped.
questions_for_user: What are the laser power at the sample and the acquisition time for each flake? Power differences change heating (redshift) and the absolute intensity, which could explain the weak C spectrum and a possible 1 to 2 cm-1 shift.
Was the spectrometer calibrated (Si at 520.7?) before each measurement? The Si line is at 519.99 to 520.02 in three spectra (-0.7 cm-1) and unusable in C, so I cannot confirm C's calibration.
Was the Si peak recorded at the same spot on C? Why is it nearly absent (a very thick flake, a different substrate region, an off-focus spot)?

Can you measure ultralow-frequency Raman (below 150 cm-1: shear about 32 cm-1 and breathing modes) or take AFM/optical contrast on C and D? These decide 4L vs 5 to 6L vs bulk, which the E2g1/A1g pair cannot.
Was the same spot measured repeatedly, and was a power series taken? Repeated exposure in air changes intensity and A1g (Bera 2017), and a power series tests heating.
Are there PL spectra, or other spectra at 633 nm or in the 1.8 to 1.9 eV range, available? They would give a thickness-independent check (A-exciton PL quenches with thickness).

limits: No thickness measurement independent of Raman (AFM, optical contrast, PL) exists here, so the layer numbers rest on one relation tabulated from one paper; D and C are not resolved from each other beyond 'at least 4L'.
Low-frequency modes (below 150 cm-1) are not covered, so layer number above about 4L, odd/even assignment and 2H vs 3R stacking cannot be tested.

One spectrum per flake: no mapping, no polarization, no power series, so uniformity, heating, strain (E2g1 splitting needs polarization) and doping cannot be separated rigorously, and they are only constrained by the absence of anomalies.

Only 514.5 nm: second-order and resonant bands (LA(M), 2LA near 450, 286/471 cm-1) are weak off resonance, so the absence of the LA(M) band is a weaker proof of low defect density than a 633 nm or UV measurement would be. No quantitative defect density (L_D) calibration was applied (not verified for MoS2).
C has no reliable Si reference (519.94 ± 0.29 cm-1), so its absolute positions are less certain than those of A, B and D, although its separation does not depend on calibration.
A1g width and Si-normalised intensity are used as supporting trends only; I did not apply a quantitative relation for them.
